lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Solar System, the Galaxy and the Inner Planets

pages.body:
On a clear night in your community, go outside and look at the sky. You will see many points of light. Most are stars, but one or two bright points that do not twinkle may be planets.

- What do you think is the difference between a star and a planet?
- Where do you think the Earth fits among all the objects you can see in the sky?

The Earth is one member of a larger family of objects held together by the Sun. In this lesson we place the Earth in the solar system, place the solar system in its galaxy and then look closely at the four planets closest to the Sun.

We begin with the Sun, which is the centre of the family we call the solar system.

questions.q: Name the star at the centre of the solar system.

parts.a: The Sun.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Sun and the solar system

pages.title: The Sun and the solar system
pages.body:
The solar system is made up of the Sun and all the objects that move around it. These include eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and dust. The Sun is a star. It is a huge ball of hot gas that gives out light and heat. Its pull of gravity is strong enough to hold every planet in its path. The Sun contains almost all of the mass of the solar system.

The eight planets in order of distance from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A useful way to remember the order is to build a sentence from the first letters of the names.

Next we move out beyond the solar system to see where it sits in space.

parts.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

lessons.title: The galaxy and the Milky Way

pages.title: The galaxy and the Milky Way
pages.body: A galaxy is a very large group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Our solar system belongs to a galaxy called the Milky Way. The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy that contains hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun is only one of them. The solar system lies in one of the spiral arms, far from the centre of the galaxy. On a very dark night away from city lights, the Milky Way appears as a faint, milky band of light across the sky, which is how it got its name.

[[pic: Drawing of the Milky Way as a spiral galaxy with an arrow pointing to the position of the solar system in one of the arms. Label the galaxy centre and the spiral arms.]]

Now we turn to the four planets nearest to the Sun, which are called the inner planets.

pages.title: The inner planets
pages.body: The inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. They are also called the terrestrial planets because, like the Earth, they have solid rocky surfaces. They are smaller and denser than the outer planets, have few or no moons and have no rings. The inner planets are separated from the giant outer planets by a wide region called the asteroid belt, which lies between Mars and Jupiter and contains many rocky objects.

| **Planet** | **Distance from the Sun** | **Time for one orbit** | **Moons** | **Special feature** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury | About 58 million km | About 88 Earth days | None | Smallest planet and closest to the Sun |
| Venus | About 108 million km | About 225 Earth days | None | Hottest planet with thick clouds |
| Earth | About 150 million km | About 365 days | One | Only known planet with life |
| Mars | About 228 million km | About 687 Earth days | Two | Red surface from iron rich rock and dust |

Finally we look at the shape of the path each planet follows.

lessons.title: The elliptical paths of the planets

pages.title: The elliptical paths of the planets
pages.body: Each planet travels around the Sun along a path called an orbit. The orbits are not perfect circles. They are ellipses, which are slightly flattened circles. The Sun is not at the exact centre of the ellipse but at a point inside it called a focus. The orbits of the inner planets are close to circular, so a drawing of the solar system that shows them as ovals can exaggerate the shape. Planets closer to the Sun move faster in their orbits and take less time to complete one trip, so a year on Mercury is much shorter than a year on Mars.

[[pic: Top view of the Sun with the four inner planets on elliptical orbits around it. Label the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars and mark the asteroid belt beyond Mars.]]

To help you remember all this, you will design and build a simple model.

pages.title: Making a model of the solar system
pages.body:
- Choose a scale that suits your space. For example, use a large ball or a drawn circle for the Sun and much smaller balls for the planets.
- Use materials from your environment such as clay, oranges, seeds, bottle tops, paper and wire.
- Place each planet in the correct order from the Sun and show the asteroid belt after Mars.
- Label each planet and write one fact beside it.
- Explain what your model shows well and what it cannot show, such as the true distances between the planets.

> **Did you know?** The distances between planets are so large that a model with correct distances cannot fit in a classroom. If the Earth were a small bead on your desk, the Sun would be a ball about one metre wide and more than one hundred metres away.

questions.q: A model of the solar system is to be built in a school compound. Explain why the planets cannot be placed at their true distances.

parts.a: The distances between planets are so large that a model with correct distances would not fit in the compound.

ideas.t: The distances between the planets are very large
A model with true distances would not fit in the space

pages.body:
Just after sunset or just before sunrise you may see a very bright light low on the horizon that does not twinkle. People have called it the morning star or the evening star, though it is not a star at all.

- What do you think this bright light could be?
- Why do you think it appears close to the Sun in the sky and is never seen at midnight?

Mercury and Venus are the two planets with orbits inside the orbit of the Earth. In this lesson we study the properties that make each of them special and describe how each one moves around the Sun.

We begin with Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun.

questions.q: An observer sees a bright object low in the west just after sunset. State which planet it may be and explain why it is not seen at midnight.

parts.a: It may be Venus, the evening star. Its orbit is inside the Earth's orbit, so it stays close to the Sun in the sky and sets soon after the Sun, so it is never seen at midnight.

ideas.t: Its orbit is inside the Earth's orbit so it stays close to the Sun
It sets soon after the Sun so it is not seen at midnight

pages.title: Properties of Mercury
pages.body:
- Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system, a little larger than the Earth's Moon.
- It is the closest planet to the Sun, at an average distance of about 58 million kilometres.
- It has no moons and no rings.
- It has almost no atmosphere, so it cannot hold heat. Its daytime surface temperature reaches about 430 degrees Celsius, while at night it falls to about 180 degrees below zero. This is one of the largest temperature ranges of any planet.
- Its surface is rocky and covered with craters, so it looks very much like the Moon.
- It has an iron rich core that makes up a large part of the planet.

Next we study Venus, the second planet from the Sun.

pages.title: Properties of Venus
pages.body:
- Venus is almost the same size as the Earth, so it is sometimes called the Earth's twin.
- It is about 108 million kilometres from the Sun.
- It has no moons and no rings.
- It is the hottest planet in the solar system, with a surface temperature of about 465 degrees Celsius, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. This is because Venus is wrapped in a thick atmosphere of mostly carbon dioxide that traps heat in a strong greenhouse effect.
- The air pressure at the surface is about ninety times that of the Earth.
- Thick clouds of sulphuric acid cover the planet. The clouds reflect sunlight very well, which is why Venus is the brightest planet in our sky.

| **Property** | **Mercury** | **Venus** |
|---|---|---|
| Position from the Sun | First | Second |
| Approximate diameter | About 4 880 km | About 12 100 km |
| Moons | None | None |
| Atmosphere | Almost none | Very thick, mostly carbon dioxide |
| Surface temperature | About 430 degrees Celsius by day and about 180 degrees below zero by night | About 465 degrees Celsius day and night |
| Special feature | Smallest planet and cratered like the Moon | Hottest planet and brightest in our sky |

Now we describe the two kinds of motion that every planet has and how they differ for these two planets.

pages.title: How Mercury and Venus move
pages.body: Every planet has two main motions. Revolution is the motion of the planet along its orbit around the Sun. Rotation is the spinning of the planet on its own axis, an imaginary line through its centre. The time to complete one revolution is the length of the planet's year. The time to complete one rotation is the planet's day.

Mercury travels fastest of all the planets and completes one revolution in about 88 Earth days. It rotates very slowly, taking about 59 Earth days to spin once on its axis. Venus completes one revolution in about 225 Earth days. It rotates even more slowly, taking about 243 Earth days to spin once. This means a day on Venus is longer than its year. Venus also rotates in the opposite direction to most planets, so on Venus the Sun would appear to rise in the west and set in the east.

[[pic: Top view showing the Sun, the orbit of Mercury and the orbit of Venus with arrows showing the direction of revolution. Add a small inset showing the spin direction of Venus opposite to the spin of the Earth.]]
To end the lesson we explain what we see in the sky.

parts.a: Mercury moves faster than Mars because it is closer to the Sun and completes one orbit in a shorter time (Mars takes 687 days).

ideas.t: Closer planets take less time to complete an orbit

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Why Mercury and Venus are seen near the Sun

pages.title: Why Mercury and Venus are seen near the Sun
pages.body:
Because the orbits of Mercury and Venus lie inside the Earth's orbit, these two planets always appear fairly close to the Sun in our sky. Venus can be seen shortly after sunset, when it is called the evening star, or shortly before sunrise, when it is called the morning star. Mercury is harder to see because it stays closer to the Sun, so it is lost in the glare for most of the year. Neither is a star. They shine by reflecting sunlight.

> **Did you know?** Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is farther from the Sun. The reason is its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere, which works like a blanket that traps heat.

questions.q: Why do Mercury and Venus appear close to the Sun in the sky?

parts.a: Their orbits lie inside the Earth's orbit, so they always appear fairly close to the Sun in the sky.

ideas.t: Their orbits lie inside the Earth's orbit
So they always appear fairly close to the Sun in the sky
